reason: This is Augustine’s compressed, hostile report, not recoverable continuous wording from Julian.
Three separated excerpts; Augustine’s intervening commentary removed.
The Bible quotations in Augustine’s ensuing answer are not Julian’s quotations.

Augustine introduces this as Julian’s advice to unlearned Christians; pronouns are adapted into readable English. The subsequent imaginary conversation with an infant’s father is Augustine’s, excluded here.

Augustine reports Julian also noted the alternative rendering perizomata, meaning coverings tied around the waist. The initial quotation about an indecent movement is Augustine’s own earlier statement, not included as Julian’s words.
Augustine says Julian quoted Horace while mocking Augustine’s interpretation of Adam and Eve’s covering. The second excerpt concerns their bodies after the transgression (Genesis 3:7).
The biblical context is Genesis 3:7. Augustine’s long answer is excluded.

The first source quotation about bodily disobedience as just repayment is Augustine’s Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.6.7, quoted as the position Julian disputes. Augustine’s subsequent biblical examples are excluded.
This is Julian’s challenge to Augustine’s argument, not advice against chastity. Augustine’s parallel hypothetical about blindness and teaching is excluded.
Augustine identifies Julian’s explanation as hyperbole. The last biblical passage is explicitly said to have been quoted by Julian; other passages introduced only in Augustine’s reply are excluded.
The context is Romans 1:24. The Sirach quotations belong to Augustine’s answer.
Augustine’s own biblical argument throughout; no discrete Julian excerpt or clearly delimited reported position.
Explains Romans 1:24. All subsequent Bible quotations and hypothetical rejoinders in this section are Augustine’s.
Only this opening quotation is attributed to Julian; the extensive exposition of election that follows is Augustine’s.
Augustine quotes this condition while challenging Julian’s reading of Romans 1:24. Psalm 140:8, the Lord’s Prayer, and James 1:14 are Augustine’s countertexts, excluded.

Julian argues conditionally against Augustine’s description of desire as punishment. Augustine’s hypothetical praise of a lying spirit is not Julian’s wording. This repeats and expands the argument in 5.3.8–9.
Augustine’s response on the soul’s origin; he says Julian turned to that question but supplies no bounded wording or developed reported claim to recover.
Augustine explicitly attributes both the biblical citation and this added comment to Julian.
The quoted words themselves are Augustine’s Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.6.7, cited by Julian; the charge of inconsistency is Julian’s reported argument.
Separated excerpts preserve both formulations which Augustine alleges conflict. Repeated partial citations of the first formulation in his answer are not duplicated.
Augustine’s surrounding quotations about bodily movement are from his own work.
Repeated statements already preserved in 5.5.20; retained here because Augustine juxtaposes these precise forms.

The first paragraph is explicitly a reported argument; the anecdote is identified as Cicero used by Julian. Augustine’s David and Saul example is excluded. Augustine also reports Julian exempted women from this particular movement; the exact scope of that exemption is unclear from the excerpt.

Separated fragments: ‘glorious struggles’ describes saints’ resistance to desire. The next three labels are Julian’s accusations quoted back against him. The final sentence preserves Augustine’s report of Julian’s charge. The rest of the section is Augustine’s response.

The final phrase repeats Julian’s description of saints’ struggle against desire. The long initial passage is Augustine quoting his own Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.6.7, excluded as independent Julian prose.

Augustine says Julian then associated this doctrine with Augustine’s statements that modesty covers what the will does not move, and that desire inflames the body on its own authority. These are Julian’s allegations about other groups, not endorsed historical descriptions.

The first conditional is adjusted from Augustine’s first-person restatement of Julian’s dilemma. The second paragraph is directly quoted. The argument is conditional upon Augustine’s characterization of desire as evil.
Entirely Augustine’s argument and biblical countertexts; no recoverable distinct Julian quotation.
Only the first sentence is quoted as Julian’s wording. Augustine’s ensuing imagined pleasure-seeker and Hortensius quotation are his own extrapolation, excluded.
The opening ‘I do not say this’ is an imagined reply supplied by Augustine, not included as Julian’s literal words. Augustine’s adaptation of Romans 12:21 is also excluded.
Julian applies this principle to marriage and sexual desire. The first source quotation is Augustine’s distinction between marriage and desire, not Julian’s original wording.
Augustine denies the allegation; it is preserved as a reported accusation, not as an established account of his teaching.

‘More modest’ is Julian’s wording for what 1 Corinthians 12:23 calls unpresentable parts. Balbus is a speaker in Cicero’s On the Nature of the Gods; only the reported appeal, not Augustine’s expansion, is recovered.
This is Julian’s reported interpretation of Augustine, who denies it. It is not continuous wording from Julian’s original work.
The source note incorrectly gives Romans 11:3; the quotation is Romans 11:33. Augustine’s earlier quotation on marital desire and his later Romans 8:14 reply are excluded.

The self-enjoyment/self-suffering passage is repeated from 5.9.35 and not duplicated here. Augustine denies the first formulation and distinguishes intercourse from fleshly disobedience; the report preserves the allegation as an allegation.
Augustine’s answer distinguishing will and pleasure; no distinct Julian quotation beyond the allegation already recovered in 5.9.36.
The Lucan poem about Cato is introduced by Augustine himself, not attributed to Julian. The general statement that Julian often cites secular writers supplies no specific fragment.
Augustine reports Julian distinguished marriage as a lesser good from continence as a greater good. Matthew 19:11 is Augustine’s counterquotation, excluded.

The claims that this would license unlimited marital indulgence are Augustine’s extrapolations, not included as Julian’s words. The subsequent Peter and Corinthians quotations belong to Augustine’s answer.
A report of Julian’s cross-reference, not a fresh surviving argument. Augustine’s analogies about adultery, theft, and the poor are excluded.
‘That kind’ refers to the religious intention of generating children for rebirth in Christ. The long Cicero quotation that follows is introduced by Augustine, not Julian.
A hostile report of Julian’s argument against inherited condemnation, not an endorsement of condemning parents.
Augustine explicitly says Julian cited this Gospel text. Augustine’s ensuing discussion of unbaptized infants and differing punishments is excluded.
The subsequent sacrificial and circumcision passages are Augustine’s counterarguments, not Julian’s quotations.

The final fragment is Julian’s charge about the implication of Augustine’s claim that all goods of marriage were fulfilled in Mary and Joseph. Augustine rejects both the charge and the proposed definition. His imagined advice to aged spouses is excluded.

Augustine interprets Julian as saying Scripture calls Mary Joseph’s wife according to public opinion rather than actuality. Luke 3:23 supplies the context of supposed parenthood, but the explicit Gospel quotations here are Augustine’s.
The second fragment is Julian’s allegation about Augustine’s position, which Augustine denies. It is not Julian’s own positive account of the first marriage.
Augustine explicitly identifies this Job passage as Julian’s evidence for the Creator’s mercy. Job 14:4–5, Matthew 5:45, and the wrath/mercy language belong to Augustine’s reply and are excluded.
Brief Augustine-only repetition about a baptized parent and an unbaptized child; no Julian quotation or distinct reported argument.

Augustine presents this as Julian’s argument from dialectic and associates it with Aristotle’s Categories. His examples of complexion, Jacob’s livestock, and Soranus are Augustine’s additions, excluded.
The last sentence is Julian’s accusation as reported in indirect speech, with its pronouns adapted. The first paragraph is not a verbatim continuous quotation.

The Sirach wording is a reported theme, not a recoverable continuous biblical quotation. The Maccabean mother’s words and Julian’s two comments are explicitly attributed. Augustine’s ensuing interpretation of the mother’s uncertainty is excluded.

The words are Augustine’s On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins 1.9.10, used by Julian as an opponent’s admission. Augustine says Julian omitted the qualifying phrase about hidden corruption of sexual desire; the report does not decide that dispute.
Augustine says Julian compared his position to this error. This is the preserved accusation, not an independent historical assessment of Apollinaris.
The source splits this allegation around Augustine’s denial; it is joined here as a reported charge.
Augustine explicitly attributes the observation on Peter to Julian. The Matthew 5:45 counterexample is Augustine’s.
‘Male sexual capacity’ renders virilitas; Augustine interprets Julian’s term as sexual desire. His James and Romans quotations belong to his reply, excluded.
Repeated three times in Augustine’s section; recorded once. The immediate referent is marital intercourse directed toward procreation, not a denial that a created free agent can later choose sin.
The first two are positions Julian attributes to Augustine, who denies them; the latter two give Julian’s conditional consequence. Proverbs and both apostolic countertexts are Augustine’s, excluded.
The topic is sexual desire. The repeated ‘glorious struggles’ formulation is noted by Augustine but already preserved at 5.6.24.
Augustine challenges the first definition; its repeated wording later in the section is not duplicated.
The long first quotation is Augustine’s own Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.15.17, not Julian’s prose; the subsequent explanation is Augustine’s answer.
Repeated forms occur several times in this section; recorded once. Julian applies the point to marital intercourse, while Augustine challenges its wider implications. Related to 5.16.59.
Pronouns in the first excerpt are adapted from Augustine’s first-person report. The second is directly addressed to Augustine.
The allegation is disputed by Augustine and is labeled accordingly. The final sentence is explicitly identified as Julian’s wording. The remaining Bible quotations belong to Augustine’s answer.
